title: Trade papers said practically unsinkable.
description:
Trade papers said practically unsinkable. Snopes quotes 1911 coverage saying the closing watertight doors made the vessel practically unsinkable. Wikipedia says three trade publications used the hedge.

White Star sold size, not safety. Snopes says its adverts called the ships the largest and finest steamers. It adds that a flyer found in 1993 said they were designed to be unsinkable as far as it is possible to do.

The walls did not reach the top. History.com says the bulkheads rose only a few feet above the waterline, so water spilled from one compartment into the next.

The lifeboat capacity. History.com puts the number aboard at 2,240.

More than 1,500 people died. She sank at about 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912. History.com says 706 survived.

The unhedged word came afterwards. On 16 April 1912 the New York Times quoted an executive of the owning group: I thought her unsinkable.

The hedge vanished. The word stuck.

Sources:
- https://www.snopes.com/history/titanic/unsinkable.asp: read via a fetch agent (page last updated 18 December 2005). Established that White Star adverts called the ships the largest and finest steamers and never made an unsinkable claim, that 1911 press coverage said the closing watertight doors made the vessel practically unsinkable, and that a White Star flyer found in February 1993 said the ships were designed to be unsinkable as far as it is possible to do.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legends_and_myths_regarding_the_Titanic: read via a fetch agent. Established that three trade publications called Titanic practically unsinkable before she sank, that she was not described as unsinkable without qualification until after the sinking, and that the New York Times of 16 April 1912 quoted an executive of the owning group saying he thought her unsinkable.
- https://www.history.com/topics/unsinkable-ships/titanic: read via a fetch agent. Established that the bulkhead walls rose only a few feet above the waterline so water spilled from one compartment to the next, that 16 boats plus four collapsibles could take 1,178 people, that 2,240 people were aboard, that more than 1,500 were lost, that 706 survived, and that she sank at about 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912.
- https://www.whoi.edu/ocean-learning-hub/ocean-topics/ocean-human-lives/underwater-archaeology/rms-titanic/history-of-rms-titanic: first 40,000 of about 55,000 characters read via a fetch agent. Confirmed lifeboat capacity of 1,178 and more than 1,500 lives lost.
